decisions.quote: In this sixth installment of Data Replicada, we report our attempt to replicate a recently published Journal of Consumer Research (JCR) article entitled, “The Impact of Resource Scarcity on Price-Quality Judgments” ( .html ). This one was full of surprises. The primary thesis of this article is straightforward: “Scarcity decreases consumers’ tendency to use price to judge product quality.” It reports six studies, three of which were conducted on MTurk. We chose to replicate Study 2A (N = 149) because it was the MTurk study with the strongest evidence, and because it also tested the effects of scarcity on two other measures: desire for abundance and categorization tendency (described below).
decisions.reason: Prior adjudication and state files were checked and are absent for this never-adjudicated work. The blind coder left authors, year, and DOI empty only because the blog post linked to the article HTML without printing its author names, publication year, or DOI in the body text. Shipped row input_row_index 2714 (Park; Lalwani; Silvera, 2019, 'The Impact of Resource Scarcity on Price-Quality Judgments', DOI 10.1093/jcr/ucz031, verified in Crossref metadata as published in Journal of Consumer Research) is the exact same original study. Note that Roux, Goldsmith, and Bonezzi (2015) is cited only as the source of the scarcity writing manipulation borrowed by the original authors, not a retested target. Thus the target is already represented by input_row_index 2714.

decisions.quote: This study is an exact replication of an experiment investigating the impacts of website design on users’ ability to use a website and their opinion of the website (Galletta et al., 2006). The replication confirms the importance of website design features, specifically delay, breadth, and familiarity on users’ ability to use and form an opinion of a website. However, the replication did not confirm the main finding, that it is the interplay of these three variables, i.e., cognitive cost, that predict performance and attitude.

corrected_value.title: Anodal-tDCS over the human right occipital cortex enhances the perception and memory of both faces and objects

decisions.location: Introduction (line 6), Experiment 1 Materials and Methods and Results/Summary of Findings (lines 11-45, specifically line 45), General Discussion (line 74), and References (line 122) of texts/e22b91e77b92663e.txt.
decisions.quote: In summary, we failed to replicate the findings of Barbieri et al. (2016), which demonstrated superior face and object perception following anodal tDCS targeting the right occipitotemporal cortex. While the pattern of results was in the predicted direction (i.e., faster RT and superior performance following anodal tDCS compared to sham), the observed effect size in the current study was small (contrasted with a medium effect size observed in Barbieri and colleagues' study) and performance was not significantly enhanced following anodal tDCS, compared to sham stimulation, in analyses of performance accuracy or reaction time.
decisions.reason: Prior adjudication and state files were checked and are absent for this never-adjudicated work. This paper reports two separate empirical replication experiments with new participant samples: Experiment 1 (n = 53: active tDCS n = 29, sham n = 24) retests Barbieri et al. (2016) (DOI 10.1016/j.neuropsychologia.2015.12.030), and Experiment 2 (n = 39: active tRNS n = 19, sham n = 20) retests Romanska et al. (2015) (DOI 10.1093/cercor/bhv016, coded as sibling target_index 1). In Experiment 1, the authors administer 1.5 mA anodal tDCS vs sham over the right occipitotemporal cortex (PO8) for 20 minutes followed by the odd-one-out face perception and object perception tasks from Barbieri et al. (2016), finding non-significant effects of tDCS condition on accuracy (F(1, 51) = 0.68, p = 0.414) and reaction time (F(1, 51) = 0.71, p = 0.404) and explicitly concluding that they failed to replicate Barbieri et al. (2016). The sole shipped row (input_row_index 2496) is Romanska; Rezlescu; Susilo; Duchaine; Banissy (2015) ('High-Frequency Transcranial Random Noise Stimulation Enhances Perception of Facial Identity', Cerebral Cortex, DOI 10.1093/cercor/bhv016). Barbieri et al. (2016) (Neuropsychologia, 81, 238-244, DOI 10.1016/j.neuropsychologia.2015.12.030) is an independent study by a completely different author team in a different journal testing a different stimulation modality (anodal tDCS rather than high-frequency tRNS), so report equivalence does not apply and it is genuinely absent from the shipped dataset.

corrected_value.authors: Watkins P, Scheer J, Ovnicek M, Kolts R.
corrected_value.title: The debt of gratitude: dissociating gratitude and indebtedness.

decisions.location: Sections 1.1.1 (line 31), 1.3 Table 1 Hypotheses 13-15 (lines 327-337), 1.5 (line 338), 3.2 (line 1207), 4.2 (line 1207), and Reference 6 (lines 1239-1245) of texts/e7746157bd29dd4b.txt.
decisions.quote: Overall, we found empirical support for the hypothesis that gratitude and indebtedness are correlated to expectation for reciprocity, yet failed to find support for the association between expectation for reciprocity and reciprocity inclination.Our findings support the argument by Watkins et al. [6] that expectation for reciprocity would be associated with higher indebtedness but lower gratitude. Provided that benevolent helping intent is associated with lower expectations for reciprocity, then according to the experimental paradigm of Watkins et al. [6], it would be associated with decreased indebtedness and increased gratitude. Our extensions help link between Tsang [1] and Watkins et al. [6] into a more comprehensive theory that higher benevolent intent is correlated with lower expectations and therefore higher gratitude than indebtedness.
decisions.reason: Prior adjudication and state files were checked and are absent for this never-adjudicated work. Although framed under the paper's 'Extensions' to Study 3 (n = 759 US Prolific participants), the authors explicitly formulate pre-registered Hypotheses 13, 14, and 15 to empirically retest the published findings of Watkins et al. (2006) [6] described in Sections 1.1.1 and 1.5—specifically that higher expectations of reciprocity are associated with decreased gratitude (H14) and increased indebtedness (H15), and that weaker expectations of reciprocity are associated with stronger willingness/inclination to reciprocate (H13). In Section 3.2, they test these hypotheses via Pearson correlations, finding support for H14 (gratitude and perceived reciprocity expectations: r(757) = -0.28, p < 0.001) and H15 (indebtedness and perceived reciprocity expectations: r(757) = 0.17, p < 0.001), but no support for H13 (reciprocity inclination and perceived reciprocity expectations: r(757) = -0.06, p = 0.08), and in Section 4.2 they explicitly compare their empirical results to Watkins et al. [6]. Per codebook rules, testing whether a specific published result holds in a new sample and comparing the results against that original qualifies as a replication target regardless of whether the section is labeled an extension. The sole shipped row (input_row_index 2243) is Tsang (2006) ('The Effects of Helper Intention on Gratitude and Indebtedness', Motivation and Emotion, DOI 10.1007/s11031-006-9031-z, sibling target_index 0). Watkins, Scheer, Ovnicek, and Kolts (2006) ('The debt of gratitude: dissociating gratitude and indebtedness', Cognition and Emotion, 20, 217-241, DOI 10.1080/02699930500172291) is a distinct original paper by different authors in a different journal and is also distinct from sibling targets 2 (Bartlett & DeSteno, 2006) and 3 (Peng et al., 2020).

decisions.location: Section 1.5 (line 338), Section 3.2 (line 1207), Section 4.3 (line 1207), and Reference 2 (lines 1215-1219) of texts/e7746157bd29dd4b.txt.
decisions.quote: Findings in the literature about the associations between gratitude and reciprocity have so far been mixed. For example, a seminal study by Bartlett & DeSteno [2] illustrated that gratitude is positively associated with reciprocity, whereas Peng et al. [16] failed to replicate Bartlett & DeSteno [2] and did not find any support for links with reciprocity for both gratitude and indebtedness. Therefore, our extension could be thought of as a conceptual replication of the Bartlett & DeSteno [2] and Peng et al. [16] directions to try and determine whether reciprocity might play a role, using an empirical design from a different study.
decisions.reason: Prior adjudication and state files were checked and are absent for this never-adjudicated work. In Sections 1.5 and 4.3, the authors explicitly state that their Study 3 extension conducts a conceptual replication contrasting the opposing published findings of Bartlett & DeSteno (2006) [2] (that gratitude is positively associated with reciprocity) and Peng et al. (2020) [16] (which found no support for links with reciprocity for both gratitude and indebtedness) using a new sample (n = 759) in Tsang's experimental design. In Section 3.2, the authors empirically test the associations of reciprocity inclination with perceived reciprocity expectations (r(757) = -0.06, p = 0.08), gratitude (r(757) = 0.52, p < 0.001), and indebtedness (r(757) = 0.29, p < 0.001), and in Section 4.3 they explicitly evaluate their results against both Bartlett & DeSteno [2] and Peng et al. [16] ('lending support for the findings by Peng et al. [16] over that of Bartlett & DeSteno [2]'). Because this paper does not re-run Peng et al.'s protocol in a linear replication chain but instead uses a third paradigm (Tsang, 2006) to directly test and adjudicate between the competing empirical claims of Bartlett & DeSteno (2006) and Peng et al. (2020), Bartlett & DeSteno (2006) is an independently retested target. It is completely distinct from the sole shipped row input_row_index 2243 (Tsang, 2006, DOI 10.1007/s11031-006-9031-z) as well as sibling targets 1 (Watkins et al., 2006) and 3 (Peng et al., 2020), and report equivalence does not apply.

corrected_value.title: Gratitude, indebtedness, and reciprocity: an extended replication of Bartlett & DeSteno (2006).

decisions.location: Section 1.5 (line 338), Section 3.2 (line 1207), Section 4.3 (line 1207), and Reference 16 (lines 1292-1298) of texts/e7746157bd29dd4b.txt.
decisions.quote: Our replication and extension takes the first step in combining the key relevant experimental paradigm of Tsang [1] and Watkins et al. [6] about the influence of helper intent and expectation for reciprocity on gratitude and indebtedness, with a conceptual replication of Bartlett & DeSteno [2] and Peng et al. [16] about the relationship between gratitude, indebtedness and reciprocity. The strong association between helper intentions and expectations for reciprocity in our findings may serve as the empirical foundation to develop a comprehensive framework for explaining the influence of helper intentions on gratitude and indebtedness. By contrast, the absence of an association between expectations for reciprocity and reciprocity inclination in our results may be seen as lending support for the findings by Peng et al. [16] over that of Bartlett & DeSteno [2].
decisions.reason: Prior adjudication and state files were checked and are absent for this never-adjudicated work. Under the codebook, an earlier replication attempt is itself a target when the current paper explicitly retests its findings. In Section 1.5, the authors state that Peng et al. (2020) [16] (an extended replication of Bartlett & DeSteno, 2006 that added indebtedness alongside gratitude) found no support for links with reciprocity for both gratitude and indebtedness, and they explicitly describe their Study 3 extension (n = 759) as 'a conceptual replication of the Bartlett & DeSteno [2] and Peng et al. [16] directions to try and determine whether reciprocity might play a role, using an empirical design from a different study' to examine 'the relationship between reciprocity inclination, gratitude and indebtedness'. They empirically test these relationships in Section 3.2 (correlating reciprocity inclination with perceived reciprocity expectations r(757) = -0.06, p = 0.08, gratitude r(757) = 0.52, p < 0.001, and indebtedness r(757) = 0.29, p < 0.001) and explicitly compare their findings to Peng et al. [16] in Section 4.3 ('lending support for the findings by Peng et al. [16] over that of Bartlett & DeSteno [2]'). Peng, Malafosse, Nelissen, and Zeelenberg (2020) (Social Influence, 15, 4-16, DOI 10.1080/15534510.2019.1710248) is an independent paper by different authors in a different journal from shipped row input_row_index 2243 (Tsang, 2006, DOI 10.1007/s11031-006-9031-z) and from sibling targets 1 (Watkins et al., 2006) and 2 (Bartlett & DeSteno, 2006), so report equivalence does not apply.
